sections.section: How do galaxies convert gas into stars? The slope of the star-formation law

claims.text: Disk-averaged total (atomic plus molecular) gas and star-formation-rate surface densities follow a super-linear global Schmidt-Kennicutt law with a power-law index near 1.4.

On sub-kiloparsec scales in nearby normal disks the star-formation-rate surface density correlates far more tightly with CO-traced molecular gas than with atomic hydrogen, and the resolved molecular relation is close to linear.

Atomic hydrogen surface density saturates near 9-10 solar masses per square parsec, above which the medium becomes molecular-dominated and below which the star-formation efficiency per unit atomic gas falls sharply in outer disks and dwarfs.

Star formation is globally inefficient, with an efficiency per free-fall time of only about 1-2 percent, and nearby molecular clouds convert gas to stars far more slowly than their free-fall times would allow.

Whether the star-formation law is intrinsically super-linear in total gas or strictly linear once the molecular phase is isolated is unresolved, with the global super-linear slope potentially an averaging artifact over the atomic-to-molecular transition.
claims.debate_topic: Linear vs super-linear star-formation law slope

claims.text: Whether molecular hydrogen is causally required for star formation or merely co-locates with shielded, cold, high-density gas is unresolved, since chemistry and turbulence models let molecule formation and gravitational collapse share the same environmental cause.
claims.debate_topic: Is H2 causal for star formation or coincidental

claims.text: Whether the star-formation efficiency per free-fall time is a low near-universal constant or varies with density, tracer, and regime is debated.
claims.debate_topic: Constant vs environment-dependent efficiency per free-fall time

claims.text: Whether suppressed star formation in outer disks reflects the failure to form shielded molecular gas or large-scale disk stability and low midplane pressure is unresolved because column density, metallicity, stellar density, and pressure covary.
claims.debate_topic: Chemical shielding vs gravitational threshold in outer disks

sections.section: What regulates a galaxy's gas supply and its position on the main sequence?

claims.text: Most star-forming galaxies occupy a narrow star-formation-rate-stellar-mass main sequence with roughly 0.3 dex scatter that persists to at least redshift 4, implying that secular accretion-regulated growth rather than mergers builds the bulk of stellar mass.
Galaxies at cosmic noon were far more gas-rich than local galaxies, with molecular gas fractions routinely 30-50 percent versus 5-10 percent today.

The molecular gas depletion time is not a single universal constant but scales systematically with specific star-formation rate and offset from the main sequence, dropping toward about 100 Myr in starbursts.
Gas-regulator or bathtub models require continuous large-scale cold accretion to sustain star formation in main-sequence galaxies over cosmic time.

Whether disks and starbursts occupy two physically distinct depletion-time sequences or a single relation varying smoothly with main-sequence offset is unresolved and tied to assumptions about the CO-to-H2 conversion factor.
claims.debate_topic: Bimodal starburst sequence vs continuous main-sequence scaling

claims.text: The magnitude and physical drivers of variation in the CO-to-H2 conversion factor are contested, with some analyses applying near-uniform values while resolved dust and dynamical calibrations find continuous variation with metallicity, radiation field, and surface density.
claims.debate_topic: Magnitude and drivers of CO-to-H2 conversion factor variation

claims.text: At fixed main-sequence offset, whether the molecular depletion time is constant or declines mildly toward higher redshift, and whether it scales with (1+z) or with the Hubble time, is unresolved within current scatter.
claims.debate_topic: Constant vs evolving depletion time and its scaling

claims.text: Gas-regulator scaling matches are necessary but not sufficient to validate feedback physics because the mass-loading factor and pristine-inflow fraction are strongly degenerate.

sections.section: Why do galaxies stop forming stars? The quenching debate

claims.text: The galaxy population is bimodal, split into a star-forming blue cloud and a quiescent red sequence, and the quiescent population has grown since redshift 2.

Reproducing the galaxy stellar mass function requires two distinct regulation regimes: strong stellar-feedback suppression in low-mass halos and additional preventive suppression of cooling in massive halos.
Stellar-mass conversion efficiency peaks near Milky-Way-scale halos of about 10^12 solar masses and falls toward both lower and higher halo mass.

Whether quenching is driven primarily by exhaustion or removal of cold gas or by kinematic and morphological suppression of star-formation efficiency in retained gas remains open, with different samples supporting different interpretations.
claims.debate_topic: Gas starvation/removal vs efficiency suppression in quenching

claims.text: Whether massive-galaxy quenching is uniquely due to radio-mode black-hole feedback or to overlapping virial-heating and environmental channels is unresolved, because the bright-end cutoff does not identify a single cause.

Offsets between the stellar metallicities of passive and star-forming galaxies have been read as favoring a prolonged reduced-inflow starvation phase over instantaneous gas removal, but the outflow contribution and timescale remain debated.

sections.section: When did the Universe form its stars? The cosmic star-formation history

claims.text: A multi-survey ultraviolet-plus-infrared synthesis of the cosmic star-formation-rate density rises to a broad maximum near redshift 2 and declines toward higher redshift, with the standard analytic fit peaking near redshift 1.9.
Under the standard cosmic history, roughly half of today's stellar mass had formed by redshift 1.3 and about one quarter above redshift 2.
Dust-obscured star formation traced in the infrared is a major and near cosmic noon dominant component of the total star-formation budget.

Whether the observed decline of star formation toward redshift above 6 is largely physical or substantially amplified by galaxies below detection limits is unresolved, because the faint-end turnover and completeness were not directly measured.

With an ultraviolet luminosity-function faint-end slope near or steeper than -2 at redshift 7, the integrated star-formation and ionizing-photon budget is extremely sensitive to the imposed faint limit.
claims.debate_topic: Faint-end extrapolation of the UV luminosity function

claims.text: Whether locally calibrated ultraviolet-slope attenuation relations apply at high redshift, or whether dust geometry and composition differ, was unsettled given inadequate far-infrared constraints for ordinary redshift-above-4 galaxies.

Whether galaxies supplied enough ionizing photons to reionize the Universe depends on an ionizing escape fraction that cannot be measured directly at redshift above 6 and on the uncertain faint-galaxy population.
claims.debate_topic: Reionization photon budget and escape fraction

claims.text: Whether a universal Salpeter- or Chabrier-like initial mass function holds across cosmic epochs or is environment- or metallicity-dependent is unresolved and propagates into every light-to-mass, star-formation, yield, and ionizing conversion.

sections.section: Do our galaxy-formation models tell us the physics? Subgrid feedback and the validation problem

claims.text: Both semi-analytic models and cosmological hydrodynamic simulations begin from hierarchical dark-matter assembly and add baryonic cooling, star formation, feedback, enrichment, and structural evolution.
Because cosmological volumes cannot resolve the multiphase interstellar medium or individual star-forming clouds, both model families require subgrid star-formation and feedback prescriptions.
The shallow abundance of low-mass galaxies relative to the halo mass function robustly requires strongly mass-dependent suppression of baryon conversion in shallow potential wells.
Distinct subgrid feedback implementations can reproduce overlapping galaxy-population statistics after calibration.

Whether reproducing observed stellar masses and star-formation rates validates the underlying regulation physics, or whether tuned agreement hides incorrect mechanisms and wrong secondary predictions, is the field's central methodological dispute.
claims.debate_topic: Calibration degeneracy: does matching observables validate physics

claims.text: Whether supernovae provide the dominant long-lived mechanical feedback budget or pre-supernova radiation, photoionization, and winds condition the birth environment enough to control the coupling is unresolved.

Whether stochastic high-temperature thermal feedback or kinetic momentum injection better represents unresolved supernova remnants and wind launch is unresolved, since both can be calibrated to work and both depend on resolution.

Whether strong winds permanently lower baryon-conversion efficiency or much of the outflowing gas recycles through galactic fountains and the circumgalactic medium is unresolved, with no universal mass-loading factor established.

Whether filamentary cold accretion dominates galaxy growth or stable virial shocks and cooling atmospheres control massive systems depends on mode definitions, mixing, feedback, and tracer observability.

Whether cosmic rays and magnetic fields provide dynamically important nonthermal pressure that drives cool winds and supports disks is unresolved because cosmic-ray transport and losses are poorly constrained.
claims.debate_topic: Cosmic-ray and magnetic support of winds and disks

sections.section: How do galaxies build their structure? Mergers, instabilities, and sizes

claims.text: Mergers, dissipative gas dynamics, and internal disk instabilities can all alter bulges, compactness, and morphology, and morphology alone does not identify which channel operated.
Gas-rich disks at cosmic noon are turbulent, with intrinsic velocity dispersions of 40-80 km/s and rotation-to-dispersion ratios of 2-6, and their central regions are strongly baryon-dominated.

Whether major and minor mergers dominate spheroid and compact-galaxy growth or violent disk instability and secular evolution contribute substantially is unresolved because morphology and simulations cannot uniquely reconstruct assembly histories.

Whether galaxy sizes largely reflect halo spin with angular-momentum retention or feedback-selective angular-momentum loss and accretion history is unresolved because direct baryon-angular-momentum accounting across phases is incomplete.
claims.debate_topic: Angular momentum vs feedback-selective loss in setting sizes

claims.text: Whether giant star-forming clumps in high-redshift disks survive feedback long enough to migrate inward and build bulges or are rapidly disrupted depends sensitively on the subgrid stellar-feedback implementation.
claims.debate_topic: Clump survival vs disruption in high-redshift disks

claims.text: Whether high-redshift disk turbulence is sustained mainly by stellar feedback or by gravitational instability and accretion is unresolved because both inject sufficient energy analytically.

sections.section: What sets a galaxy's metal content? The mass-metallicity and fundamental relations

claims.text: Local star-forming galaxies show a positive gas-phase mass-metallicity relation that steepens below about 10^10.5 solar masses, flattens above it, and has roughly 0.1 dex scatter.

At fixed stellar mass, local gas-phase metallicity is associated with star-formation rate, and a mass-star-formation-rate-metallicity surface reduces residual scatter relative to the two-variable relation.

Consistently calibrated samples show lower gas-phase abundance at fixed stellar mass toward higher redshift, and JWST/NIRSpec extends the relation to low-mass galaxies at redshift 4-10 that lie below local samples.

Strong-line, electron-temperature, recombination-line, and photoionization-model metallicity calibrations can shift inferred oxygen abundances by as much as 0.7 dex and do not share one settled absolute scale, so normalizations are comparable only when the underlying scale is matched.

The existence, strength, and redshift invariance of a universal mass-star-formation-rate-metallicity relation are disputed, with some matched analyses finding no evolution to redshift 3.3 while other data and simulations indicate substantial offsets at higher redshift.

The mass-metallicity relation alone cannot separate mass-dependent outflow, inflow dilution, star-formation efficiency, recycling, and enriched reaccretion, since several regulator and simulation parameter combinations reproduce it.

Which metallicity scale transfers to early galaxies is unresolved, as local calibrations disagree in normalization and applying some of them to early galaxies can bias inferred oxygen abundance downward.

sections.section: How do galaxies assemble their chemical elements? Chemical evolution

claims.text: Cosmic chemical enrichment is a long-term balance among pristine inflow, star-formation efficiency, and metal-loaded outflows, because closed-box models cannot reproduce the metallicity distribution of long-lived low-mass stars (the G-dwarf problem).
The Type Ia supernova delay-time distribution follows a declining power law of about t^-1.07 over billions of years, making Type Ia supernovae the dominant source of delayed iron enrichment.
The nitrogen-to-oxygen ratio shows a low-abundance plateau consistent with primary nitrogen and rises steeply at high abundance where secondary nitrogen dominates.
Local star-forming disks generally show negative radial gas-phase metallicity gradients consistent with inside-out assembly, with a characteristic slope of order -0.1 dex per effective radius.

Whether the [alpha/Fe] ratio is a clean star-formation-timescale clock is debated, since a top-heavy initial mass function or metallicity-dependent yields could raise it independently of the star-formation history.

The progenitor channel of Type Ia supernovae is debated, as the single-degenerate scenario produces prompt explosions but struggles with the late delay tail while the double-degenerate merger scenario yields the tail but too few prompt events.

The JWST detection of a supersolar nitrogen-to-oxygen ratio in GN-z11 at redshift 10.6 is in tension with standard delayed nitrogen enrichment and has prompted competing explanations invoking Wolf-Rayet winds, tidal disruption events, or dense stellar clusters.

Whether high-redshift disks have steeper, flat, or inverted radial metallicity gradients is debated, as observed gradients at redshift 1-3 are diverse and may reflect genuine cold-flow accretion and feedback or observational beam-smearing.

sections.section: Where are the baryons and metals? The cosmic census and baryon cycle

claims.text: Big-Bang-nucleosynthesis and cosmic-microwave-background estimates give concordant total cosmic baryon densities, but this fixes the total, not where the baryons later reside.
More than 90 percent of present-day cosmic baryons remain gaseous rather than locked in stars.

The comoving atomic-gas density evolves only modestly from redshift 5 to today, while the molecular-gas density rises toward cosmic noon and declines afterward, tracking the star-formation-rate density.

Whether adding stars, cold gas, dust, and ionized gas brings the cosmic metal census near closure or whether residual metals hide in poorly measured warm-hot phases is contested, turning on uncertain yields and ionization corrections.
The weak evolution of the atomic-gas density could be biased by absorber column thresholds, the rarity of high-column systems, and dust-obscured sightlines missing from optical quasar samples.
Whether CO luminosity functions directly yield the cosmic molecular-gas density or whether uncertain excitation and metallicity-dependent conversion undermine those masses is unresolved.
Different initial mass functions, solar abundance scales, and nucleosynthetic yields shift the expected metal budget against which every closure calculation is compared.
claims.debate_topic: Metal yield and IMF systematics in the census

sections.section: What is the circumgalactic medium doing? The halo gas reservoir

claims.text: The circumgalactic medium is multiphase in ionization and complex in kinematics, so a line-of-sight velocity does not uniquely map to radius.
Strong O VI absorption is widespread around star-forming L-star galaxies and much weaker around passive ones.

Photoionization modeling implies a large cool circumgalactic reservoir of order 10^10-10^11 solar masses around L-star galaxies, and roughly 75-80 percent of the metals produced by L-star galaxies reside outside their stellar disks.

Whether large cool and warm reservoirs account for the halo baryon budget or whether a hot low-density phase remains unmeasured so closure is not demonstrated depends decisively on radial extrapolation, metallicity, and X-ray density-profile assumptions.

Whether O VI arises in collisionally ionized gas near 10^5.3-10^5.6 K or in photoionized and non-equilibrium interfaces and cooling flows is unresolved, because one O VI column does not fix density, temperature, path length, or mass.
claims.debate_topic: Origin and temperature of O VI

claims.text: Whether cool clouds are rapidly shredded by hydrodynamic instabilities in the hot halo or survive and grow aided by cooling, suppressed conduction, or magnetic fields is unresolved because cloud sizes and interfaces are unresolved observationally and numerically.

Whether low-metallicity cool gas marks fresh accretion and high-metallicity gas marks recycled outflow, or whether mixing and ionization blend the origins so metallicity alone cannot reconstruct a trajectory, is unresolved.
claims.debate_topic: Cool-CGM origin: accretion vs recycled winds

claims.text: Classifying individual circumgalactic absorbers as inflow or outflow is degenerate, because projection and recycling blur the geometric and kinematic clues.
claims.debate_topic: Inflow vs outflow identification in the CGM

claims.text: Different wind loading, velocity, and recycling prescriptions yield different circumgalactic columns and phase masses, so galaxy-integrated calibration does not uniquely constrain halo-scale gas histories.
